abstract: Graphic abstract ADAM8 in cardiac macrophages was upregulated during myocardial infarction (MI), which promoted its binding with ANXA2. This interaction subsequently led to ANXA2 phosphorylation at the Ser26 site, ultimately facilitating mTOR phosphorylation at the Ser2448 site. This cascade of events inhibited autophagy activation, increased the expression of IL-1β, IL-18, and TNF-α, and decreased the secretion of VEGFA. These combined effects suppressed angiogenesis, promoted inflammation in the infarcted area, and ultimately exacerbated post-MI cardiac dysfunction (depicted on the left in blue). Notably, knocking out ADAM8 in macrophages hindered ANXA2 phosphorylation at the Ser26 site, inhibited the subsequent phosphorylation of mTOR at the Ser2448 site, activated the autophagy pathway, and improved myocardial injury in mice after MI (depicted on the right in pink). Materials and methods
Patient enrollment
In total, 90 patients with or without AMI were enrolled in this study from the Cardiology Department of Zhongda Hospital, Southeast University, during May 2019–May 2021. There were 20 patients in the non-MI group and 70 patients in the AMI group. This single-center, observational study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhongda Hospital affiliated with Southeast University, Nanjing, China (Number: 2018ZDSYLL134-P01). Blood plasma and basic characteristics were collected from patients (
Supplemental Table 1
). Inclusion criteria were as follows: 1. Willing to participate in the study and signed an informed consent form; 2. Males or non-pregnant females over 18 years of age; 3. AMI group: typical chest pain symptoms, elevated TnI, and ischemic ST-T changes on electrocardiogram. Non-MI group: patients without MI. Exclusion criteria were as follows: 1. Severe liver or kidney disease (not caused by heart disease); 2. Uncontrolled severe hypertension (systolic blood pressure > 180 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure > 100 mmHg after standardized treatment); 3. History of ischemic stroke within 1 week, intracranial hemorrhage, gastrointestinal bleeding within 6 months, or surgery within 30 days; 4. Severe respiratory distress, such as bronchial asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; 5. Other serious diseases with a life expectancy of less than six months; 6. Sick sinus syndrome, second or third degree atrioventricular block, or history of syncope due to bradycardia; 7. Pregnant or lactating women; 8. Other situations in which the study participant was considered unsuitable for this study.
Animals and treatments
All animal experiments conformed to animal experimental ethics rules and were approved by the Animal Care & Welfare Committee of Southeast University (Number: 20200326014). All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the US National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8th Edition, 2011). Macrophage-specific ADAM8-KO mice on a C57BL/6 background (Cyagen Biosciences, Suzhou, China) were generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 system (
Supplemental Fig.1
). Mice were bred and maintained in the Southeast University Laboratory Animal Center, and six- to ten-week-old male mice were used in this study. Randomization and allocation concealment were performed, and the operators of animal experiments were blinded to the group allocation. Murine MI models were created by ligating the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. Briefly, mice were anesthetized with sodium pentobarbital (1 %, 50 mg/kg weight) by intraperitoneal injection and mechanically ventilated with a small animal ventilator (ALC-V8S, Shanghai, China). Next, mice were subjected to thoracotomy, and LAD segments were permanently ligated with 6–0 monofilament nylon sutures at approximately 2 mm below the tip of the left auricle. Blanching of the myocardium distally from the ligature was considered successful complete occlusion. Subsequently, the air was exhausted, and the chest wall was closed.
Culture and treatment of mouse BMDMs
BMDMs were extracted, cultured and treatment according to previous researches
[30]
,
[31]
. Mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation after being anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (1 %, 50 mg/kg weight). Then, mice were soaked in 75 % alcohol for 5 min and transferred to a clean area. The skin of mice hindlimbs of the mice was removed, and the femur was cut off and placed in a PBS culture dish. Muscle was removed with tweezers and scissors, and the femur and tibia were removed aseptically. After the joint was cut off, a 1 mL syringe filled with DMEM was used to puncture the bone marrow cavity for repeated rinsing. The bone marrow solution was passed through a 40-μm cell strainer into a 50 mL centrifuge tube. Then, the solution was centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded. Three to five mL of sterile mouse red blood cell lysis buffer was added for incubation at room temperature for 2 min. The solution was again centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded. The cell precipitate was resuspended in DMEM containing M−CSF (20 ng/mL) (HY-P7085, MedChemExpress) at a final concentration of 1 × 10
6
/mL. The cell suspension was transferred to a culture plate (Day 0), and the culture medium containing M−CSF (20 ng/mL) was replaced on Day 3. Induction was considered successful on Day 7. LPS (1μg/mL for 12 h) was utilized to induce pro-inflammatory macrophages for simulating the microenvironment after MI, while IL-4 (20 ng/mL for 12 h) was employed to induce anti-inflammatory macrophages
[31]
.
Culture and treatment of peritoneal macrophages from mice
The abdominal cavities of mice were injected with 1.5 mL of 3 % mercaptoacetate culture medium. After 3 days, the abdominal cavities were rinsed with pre-cooled PBS, and the liquid was placed in a 50 mL centrifuge tube. After centrifugation at 1500 rpm for 10 min at 4 ℃, the supernatant was discarded. Cells were resuspended in DMEM containing 10 % FBS, counted and seeded in culture plates. After 24 h of cultivation, the culture medium was discarded, and the cells were washed twice with PBS. Fresh DMEM containing 10 % FBS was added for the subsequent experiments.

Then, 1 mL of heart digestion solution was added to a 2 mL centrifuge tube, and the heart tissue was cut into small pieces as much as possible. Digestion was carried out at 37 °C for 1 h to produce a single-cell suspension. The suspension was filtered through a 40 μm cell strainer, neutralized with double the volume of complete medium, centrifuged at 1200 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded. Finally, red blood cells were lysed using a red blood cell lysis solution, washed with PBS, and the cell suspension was obtained. CD45

and F4/80

magnetic beads (Cat# 130–052-301 and 130-110-443, Militenyi Biotec, Germany) were purchased, and the single-cell suspension was passed through columns in sequence according to the instructions to obtain CD45
+

cardiac macrophages.
RNA isolation and quantitative RT-PCR
After the supernatant was discarded from 6-well plates, BMDMs were washed with PBS twice. A total of 500 µL of TRIZOL was added to each well, cells were digested for 3 min, and the liquid was placed in an Eppendorf tube. The solution was mixed well and left to incubate for 3 min. Then, 1/5 vol of chloroform (100 µL) was added, mixed vigorously for 15 s, and the solution was incubated at room temperature for 5 min. Tubes were centrifuged at 12000 rpm for 15 min, and the supernatant (colorless aqueous phase) was placed in an Eppendorf tube. Then, 0.5 mL of isopropanol, was added and incubated for 10 min at room temperature. After centrifugation at 12000 rpm for 10 min, the supernatant was discarded, leaving a white RNA deposit at the bottom of the tube. Subsequently, the RNA deposit was washed with 1 mL of 75 % ethanol, followed by centrifugation at 7500 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was removed, and the sample was placed on ice for 5–10 min to dry the RNA. Then, 20–30 µL of DEPC water was added, mixed well, and aliquoted into PCR tubes. According to the reverse transcription reagent manual (R323, Vazyme, Nanjing, China), genomic DNA was removed, a reverse transcription reaction system was prepared, and a reverse transcription reaction was performed. Next, qPCR was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Q711, Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The relative primer sequences were listed in
Supplemental Material 1
.
Western blotting
A prepared gel was loaded in an electrophoresis system, and protein samples were added to each well. Electrophoresis was performed at a constant voltage of 120 V. After the bromophenol blue dye reached the bottom of the gel, electrophoresis was stopped. The gel was removed and subjected to rapid membrane transfer at a constant current of 400 mA for 30 min. After removal, the membranes were blocked in milk or 5 %BSA for 1 h. Membranes were then incubated with the corresponding primary antibody at 4 ℃ overnight. Next, membranes were placed on a shaker and washed three times with TBST three times for 5 min. Membranes were incubated with the corresponding secondary antibody on a shaker at room temperature for 60 min and then washed three times with TBST for 10 min. Finally, membranes were exposed using a fully automatic chemiluminescence image analyzer (Tanon 5200, Shanghai, China), and ImageJ software was used for analysis and statistical analysis. The antibodies used were listed in
Supplemental Material 1
.
Histological analysis
Paraffin sections of mouse heart tissue were dewaxed in water, followed by overnight potassium dichromate staining and iron hematoxylin staining. The tissues were then subjected to acid fuchsin phosphomolybdate staining and aniline blue staining. Finally, the sections were dehydrated, sealed, and scanned with a digital slice scanning machine.
Immunofluorescence analysis
Heart tissue was embedded in paraffin and cut into sections. Paraffin sections were dewaxed in water and subjected to antigen repair. A PAP Pen circle was used to prevent antibody flow. BSA was used for blocking purposes, and the corresponding primary antibody was added for incubation in a wet box at 4 °C overnight. Sections were incubated in PBS and placed on a decolorization shaker to rinse the samples. The secondary antibody was then added and sections were incubated at room temperature for 1 h. DAPI was used to stain the nucleus, and a spontaneous fluorescence quenching agent was added. Finally, an anti-fluorescence quenching agent was added, and the sections were sealed. Sections were imaged and scanned using a Digital Pathology System (3DHISTECH, Hungary).
Bone marrow transplantation
Eight-week-old KO mice were treated with antibiotic water (ampicillin, 1 mg/mL) for 1 week and then irradiated with 8.5 Gy (Co-60 radiation source; provided by the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, China). Eight-week-old Flox and KO mice were used as donors. Donor mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation after anesthesia induction with an intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (1 %, 50 mg/kg weight). Bone marrow cells were collected from the femur and tibia and resuspended in DMEM without FBS and counted. At fourth hour after bone marrow irradiation, 1 × 10
7
bone marrow cells from the donor mice were injected into the recipient mice via the tail vein, and the recipient mice continued to receive antibiotic water for one week. Gene identification was performed 6 weeks after transplantation. BMDM transplantation was validated using flow cytometry after their transfer from CD45.2 mice to CD45.1 mice

,
[33]
.
Construction of AAV for macrophage-specific ADAM8 overexpression
An AAV vector for ADAM8 overexpression was constructed with GV649 as the vector, macrophage-specific marker CD68 as the promoter, and the fusion 3Flag sequence vector (pAAV-CD68p-MCS-EGFP-3Flag-SV40 PolyA), cloned at BamHI/BamHI. The plasmids were cloned, the ADAM8 sequence fragment was amplified, and the sequence fragment was inserted into the vector. Then, the virus was packaged, purified, subjected to titer testing, and stored at −80 C (Genechem Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China). 4- to 6-week-old male mice were injected with 8 × 10
11
v.g. of the ADAM8 overexpression AAV through the tail vein. After the mice were fed for 4 weeks, the overexpression efficiency was verified by western blot analysis, and MI models were established. After another 4 weeks, the mice were sacrificed for further examination.

Adenoviruses with sustained activation or inactivation of phosphorylation sites targeting Anxa2 (S26D and S26A) were constructed (OBiO Technology Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China). The vector with phosphorylation activation was Anxa2 (S26D), and the vector with phosphorylation inactivation was Anxa2 (S26A). The vector names for Anxa2 (S26D) and Anxa2 (S26A) were pcADV-EF1-mNeonGreen-CMV-Anxa2(S26D)-3xFLAG and pcADV-EF1-mNeonGreen-CMV-Anxa2(S26A)-3xFLAG.
Echocardiography
Mice were anesthetized with a combination of 1.5 % isoflurane and 0.5 L/min of 100 % O
2
, followed by depilation to prepare the skin. The parasternal left ventricular long axis section was used; the ultrasonic probe was placed at the left ventricular papillary muscle position, and the probe position was moved to obtain a clearer image. M−mode ultrasonic images were collected. Ultrasonic analysis software was used to measure and calculate the cardiac function indexes of mice from each group, including heart rate (HR), fractional shortening (FS), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular end diastolic volume (LVEDV), and left ventricular end systolic volume (LVESV).
RNA extraction, library construction, and sequencing
Total RNA was extracted using a TTRIZOL reagent kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA quality was assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA) and RNase free agarose gel electrophoresis. After total RNA was extracted, mRNA was enriched with Oligo(dT) beads. Then, the enriched mRNA was fragmented into short fragments using fragmentation buffer and reverse transcribed into cDNA using NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB #7530, New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA). The purified double-stranded cDNA fragments were end repaired, and A base was added and ligated to Illumina sequencing adapters. The ligation reaction was purified with AMPure XP Beads (1.0X). Ligated fragments were subjected to size selection by agarose gel electrophoresis and PCR amplified. The resulting cDNA library was sequenced using Illumina Novaseq6000 by Gene Denovo Biotechnology Co. (Guangzhou, China).
Proteomics
Proteins were extracted from the samples and digested enzymatically. Quality control was performed on the samples before mass spectrometry detection. The data obtained from the DDA acquisition mode were used to build a database using Pulsar software. The DIA data results were analyzed using the DDA reference database to identify the proteins. If at least one sample had a detected protein, the qualitative result of the protein and its quantitative results for all samples were output. The qualitative protein analysis required that the identification standards of Precursor Threshold 1.0 % FDR and Protein Threshold 1.0 % FDR at the peptide and protein levels, respectively, were met. Regarding protein quantification, normalization was performed first, and the average peak area of the top 3 MS1 peptides with an FDR less than 1.0 % was selected for protein quantification (GENE DENOVO, Guangzhou, China).
Co-immunoprecipitation/mass spectrometry
(COIP/MS)
Immunoprecipitation was performed using an anti-ADAM8 antibody (IP: ADAM8) or IgG (IP: IgG) and H293T cells, and the protein lysates were used for Shotgun LC-MS/MS (Genechem Co., Ltd, Shanghai). Immunoprecipitation was also performed with the anti-ADAM8 antibody (IP: ADAM8) or IgG (IP: IgG) and RAW264.7 cells, and the protein lysates were used for LC-MS/MS (Applied Protein Technology Co. Ltd, Shanghai). Protein solutions were digested with proteases to generate a mixture of peptides, which were then separated by high-performance liquid chromatography and analyzed by tandem mass spectrometry. Peptides ionized in a mass spectrometer carry a certain amount of charge, allowing for the determination of their mass-to-charge ratio (
m
/
z
) through the detector. Additionally, peptides were subjected to further ionization and fragmentation in a mass spectrometer, resulting in second-order mass spectrometry signals. By using retrieval software and relevant protein databases, the mass spectrometry data obtained could be analyzed to reconstruct the protein composition of the sample. COIP validation of binding between ADAM8 and ANXA2 was also performed using anti-ADAM8 antibody (IP: ADAM8), ANXA2 antibody (IP: ANXA2), or IgG (IP: IgG) and RAW 264.7 cells. Immunoblotting with anti-ADAM8 and anti-ANXA2 antibodies was performed.
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
(ELISA)
Cell culture supernatants and human plasma samples were centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 20 min at 2–8 ℃ to remove impurities and cell debris. An ELISA was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Wuhan, China), and the optical density (OD) value was measured at a wavelength of 450 nm.
siRNA transfection
siRNA transfection was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (GenePharma, Shanghai, China). The siRNA-Mate transfection reagent was placed at room temperature and gently mixed before use. Next, 100 μL of DMEM (serum-free and antibiotic-free medium) was added to sterile Eppendorf tubes. The appropriate siRNA was added to the Eppendorf tube and mixed thoroughly. Then, the appropriate siRNA-Mate transfection reagent was added and rapidly swirled for 10 s to completely mix. After incubation at room temperature for 10 min, a transfection complex of siRNA and the transfection reagent formed. The cell culture plate was loaded with 0.5 mL of preheated fresh culture medium in each well, and the transfection mixture was added. Then, cells were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h and ANXA2 was knocked down in BMDMs by means of siRNA transfection.
Statistics
The sample size of patients in the clinical cohort and that of mice used in the study was determined based on similar published articles. Strict exclusion criteria were implemented to control confounding factors in the clinical cohort, thereby enhancing the credibility of the study results. Mouse littermates were randomly allocated to different groups, and investigators were blinded to group allocation. SPSS 26.0, GraphPad Prism 9.5.0, and MedCalc 15.0 software were used for data analysis. For continuous data, the data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation. If the data satisfy both normal distribution and homogeneity of variance, the unpaired
t
-test is used for comparisons between two groups, and One-way ANOVA along with Tukey's multiple comparisons test or Student-Newman-Keuls test are employed for comparing more than two groups. If the data satisfy normal distribution but not homogeneity of variance, the unpaired
t
-test with Welch's correction is used for comparisons between two groups, and Welch's ANOVA test is applied for comparisons among multiple groups. If the data do not satisfy normal distribution, the Mann Whitney test is used for comparisons between two groups, and the Kruskal-Wallis test is employed for comparisons among multiple groups. For categorical variables, the chi-squared test was used for comparison. Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the differences between two survival curves were compared using the log-rank test. Statistical details were listed in the
Supplemental Material 2
. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Introduction
Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a significant global health burden, with over 7 million people worldwide suffering from it each year
[1]
. The occurrence of MI leads to myocardial ischemia and damage-related molecular pattern (DAMP) release by necrotic cells, after which, inflammatory cells such as macrophages and neutrophils are recruited to the infarcted area of the heart
[2]
. Within hours after the onset of MI, these inflammatory cells begin the post-MI inflammatory phase. Subsequently, proliferated inflammatory macrophages derived from monocytes clear the damaged tissues. At 3–7 days after MI, the number of cardiac macrophages reaches a peak, and inflammatory macrophages and myofibroblasts mediate post-MI myocardial fibrosis and scar formation
[3]
,
[4]
.
MI severely damages the coronary microcirculation, leading to vascular collapse and sparse capillaries in the infarcted area. Post-MI, a strong angiogenic response is imperative for cardiac repair, which starts in the infarct boundary area and extends to the necrotic infarct core. Populations of macrophages and fibroblast populations are the main driving factors of this angiogenesis response. Animal studies have shown that an enhanced endogenous angiogenesis response after MI can reduce scar formation and adverse left ventricular remodeling. In humans experiencing MI, microvessel formation occurs in the infarcted area at 4 days after MI and peaks around two weeks after MI
[5]
,
[6]
,
[7]
.
Macrophages are directly and indirectly involved in regulating angiogenesis in healthy and diseased tissues
[8]
. Ferraro, et al. found reduced cardiac function and proinflammatory macrophage accumulation in AnxA1-/- mice. VEGFA release was impaired in AnxA1-/- cardiac macrophages, and ANXA1 treatment increased VEGFA release and improved cardiac function
[9]
. A study performed by Revelo, et al. utilizing single-cell RNA sequencing of cardiac immune cells isolated from transverse aortic constriction hearts showed that cardiac resident macrophages can stimulate angiogenesis and inhibit fibrosis when undergoing cardiac pressure overload
[10]
. Macrophage ectoenzymes, such as CD39 and CD73, can rapidly convert ATP into adenosine, which can reduce inflammatory mediator production and induce growth-related and angiogenic factor production via high affinity adenosine receptors
[11]
.
A disintegrin and metalloproteinase 8 (ADAM8) may participate in the occurrence and development of respiratory diseases and pancreatic tumors, but its role in cardiovascular diseases remains unclear
[12]
. ADAM8 was first discovered in macrophages in mice
[13]
, and subsequently confirmed to exist in THP-1 human macrophage
[14]
. ADAM8 consists of different functional domains, including an N-terminal prodomain, metalloproteinase domain, disintegrin (DIS) domain, cysteine-rich domain, epidermal growth factor (EGF)-like domain, transmembrane (TM) domain, and cytoplasmic tail
[15]
. These domains are responsible for different functions, such as autocatalytic activity, shedding, and signaling transduction
[16]
. The pro-domain plays a crucial role in protecting enzyme activity, thus ensuring proper enzyme folding, and guiding it into the secretory pathway
[17]
. Through the cysteine switch mechanism, it maintains the metalloprotease site in a non-active state before the catalytic domain is activated, thereby working like a competitive inhibitor
[18]
. The metalloprotease domain is the main active region of ADAM8, giving it with the ability to cleave the extracellular portions of ligands, receptors, and signaling molecules on the cell surface
[19]
. This cleavage has profound effects on cell signaling pathways, cell differentiation, proliferation, and growth-related processes
[20]
. However, the metalloprotease activity of ADAM8 may require autolytic processing for activation. The disintegrin-like domain plays a significant role in regulating cell adhesion and signal transduction. Although ADAM8 lacks a typical RGD motif, it possesses a unique RX6DLPEF sequence that can bind to specific integrins (such as α9β1), thereby mediating the interaction between cells and the extracellular matrix or between cells, including mediating the functions of ADAM8 that are independent of its proteolytic activity
[21]
,
[22]
. The cysteine-rich domain may participate in protein–protein interactions and signal transduction
[23]
. Together with the metalloprotease domain, it may play a synergistic role in cell migration and adhesion, thereby providing additional proteolytic activity to ADAM8
[24]
. The EGF-like domain is commonly found in secreted or transmembrane proteins that anchor proteins to the cell surface
[25]
. Regarding ADAM8, it may be involved in substrate recognition and enzyme activation processes, contributing to the localization and function of ADAM8 on the cell surface
[24]
. The transmembrane domain firmly anchors ADAM8 to the cell membrane, allowing it to perform its biological functions on the cell surface. It may interact with other transmembrane proteins to jointly regulate the activity and function of ADAM8
[26]
. The cytoplasmic tail domain plays a vital role in regulating the stability and protein levels of ADAM8. It may participate in intracellular signal transduction and regulatory processes, thereby affecting the distribution and function of ADAM8 within the cell.
The ADAM family is closely related to the regulation of macrophage function
[27]
. ADAM8, as a multifunctional molecule, plays a crucial role in cell adhesion, signal transduction, and proteolysis, and its unique activation mechanism further highlights its complexity and importance in biological processes and disorders
[15]
. Previous studies have reported that ADAM8 knockout significantly reduces the levels of TNF-α, IL-10, and IL-12 secreted by bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) stimulated with LPS
[16]
. Both ADAM8 knockout and pharmacological inhibition significantly improve lung injury in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
[28]
. In microglia, the cytoplasmic tail region of ADAM8 interacts with Fra-1 (a protein encoded by Fosl-1), stabilizes the phosphorylated state of Fra-1, upregulates Map3k4 expression, thereby exacerbating neuroinflammation during spinal cord injury in mice
[29]
.
In this study, ADAM8 plasma levels were measured in AMI patients and macrophage ADAM8 expression at different times after AMI onset.
In vivo
experiments with genetic knockout (KO) and adeno-associated virus (AAV) overexpression of ADAM8, as well as bone marrow transplantation, showed that ADAM8 aggravated heart injury after MI. Pharmacological inhibition with bevacizumab decreased the survival rate improvement in ADAM8 KO mice.
In vitro
experiments showed that ADAM8 in macrophages binds to Annexin A2 (ANXA2), promoting Ser26 phosphorylation; this further inhibits the autophagy pathway, decreases the secretion of the angiogenic factor VEGFA, and increases the secretion of the inflammatory factors IL-1β and IL-18. Here, we not only demonstrated the role of macrophage ADAM8 in AMI but also elucidated the specific mechanism of angiogenesis and regulation of inflammation.

RNA isolation and quantitative RT-PCR
After the supernatant was discarded from 6-well plates, BMDMs were washed with PBS twice. A total of 500 µL of TRIZOL was added to each well, cells were digested for 3 min, and the liquid was placed in an Eppendorf tube. The solution was mixed well and left to incubate for 3 min. Then, 1/5 vol of chloroform (100 µL) was added, mixed vigorously for 15 s, and the solution was incubated at room temperature for 5 min. Tubes were centrifuged at 12000 rpm for 15 min, and the supernatant (colorless aqueous phase) was placed in an Eppendorf tube. Then, 0.5 mL of isopropanol, was added and incubated for 10 min at room temperature. After centrifugation at 12000 rpm for 10 min, the supernatant was discarded, leaving a white RNA deposit at the bottom of the tube. Subsequently, the RNA deposit was washed with 1 mL of 75 % ethanol, followed by centrifugation at 7500 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was removed, and the sample was placed on ice for 5–10 min to dry the RNA. Then, 20–30 µL of DEPC water was added, mixed well, and aliquoted into PCR tubes. According to the reverse transcription reagent manual (R323, Vazyme, Nanjing, China), genomic DNA was removed, a reverse transcription reaction system was prepared, and a reverse transcription reaction was performed. Next, qPCR was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Q711, Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The relative primer sequences were listed in
Supplemental Material 1
.
Western blotting
A prepared gel was loaded in an electrophoresis system, and protein samples were added to each well. Electrophoresis was performed at a constant voltage of 120 V. After the bromophenol blue dye reached the bottom of the gel, electrophoresis was stopped. The gel was removed and subjected to rapid membrane transfer at a constant current of 400 mA for 30 min. After removal, the membranes were blocked in milk or 5 %BSA for 1 h. Membranes were then incubated with the corresponding primary antibody at 4 ℃ overnight. Next, membranes were placed on a shaker and washed three times with TBST three times for 5 min. Membranes were incubated with the corresponding secondary antibody on a shaker at room temperature for 60 min and then washed three times with TBST for 10 min. Finally, membranes were exposed using a fully automatic chemiluminescence image analyzer (Tanon 5200, Shanghai, China), and ImageJ software was used for analysis and statistical analysis. The antibodies used were listed in
Supplemental Material 1
.
Histological analysis
Paraffin sections of mouse heart tissue were dewaxed in water, followed by overnight potassium dichromate staining and iron hematoxylin staining. The tissues were then subjected to acid fuchsin phosphomolybdate staining and aniline blue staining. Finally, the sections were dehydrated, sealed, and scanned with a digital slice scanning machine.
Immunofluorescence analysis
Heart tissue was embedded in paraffin and cut into sections. Paraffin sections were dewaxed in water and subjected to antigen repair. A PAP Pen circle was used to prevent antibody flow. BSA was used for blocking purposes, and the corresponding primary antibody was added for incubation in a wet box at 4 °C overnight. Sections were incubated in PBS and placed on a decolorization shaker to rinse the samples. The secondary antibody was then added and sections were incubated at room temperature for 1 h. DAPI was used to stain the nucleus, and a spontaneous fluorescence quenching agent was added. Finally, an anti-fluorescence quenching agent was added, and the sections were sealed. Sections were imaged and scanned using a Digital Pathology System (3DHISTECH, Hungary).
Bone marrow transplantation
Eight-week-old KO mice were treated with antibiotic water (ampicillin, 1 mg/mL) for 1 week and then irradiated with 8.5 Gy (Co-60 radiation source; provided by the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, China). Eight-week-old Flox and KO mice were used as donors. Donor mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation after anesthesia induction with an intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (1 %, 50 mg/kg weight). Bone marrow cells were collected from the femur and tibia and resuspended in DMEM without FBS and counted. At fourth hour after bone marrow irradiation, 1 × 10
7
bone marrow cells from the donor mice were injected into the recipient mice via the tail vein, and the recipient mice continued to receive antibiotic water for one week. Gene identification was performed 6 weeks after transplantation. BMDM transplantation was validated using flow cytometry after their transfer from CD45.2 mice to CD45.1 mice

.
Construction of AAV for macrophage-specific ADAM8 overexpression
An AAV vector for ADAM8 overexpression was constructed with GV649 as the vector, macrophage-specific marker CD68 as the promoter, and the fusion 3Flag sequence vector (pAAV-CD68p-MCS-EGFP-3Flag-SV40 PolyA), cloned at BamHI/BamHI. The plasmids were cloned, the ADAM8 sequence fragment was amplified, and the sequence fragment was inserted into the vector. Then, the virus was packaged, purified, subjected to titer testing, and stored at −80 C (Genechem Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China). 4- to 6-week-old male mice were injected with 8 × 10
11
v.g. of the ADAM8 overexpression AAV through the tail vein. After the mice were fed for 4 weeks, the overexpression efficiency was verified by western blot analysis, and MI models were established. After another 4 weeks, the mice were sacrificed for further examination.
Construction of adenovirus with sustained activation or inactivation of phosphorylation sites
Adenoviruses with sustained activation or inactivation of phosphorylation sites targeting Anxa2 (S26D and S26A) were constructed (OBiO Technology Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China). The vector with phosphorylation activation was Anxa2 (S26D), and the vector with phosphorylation inactivation was Anxa2 (S26A). The vector names for Anxa2 (S26D) and Anxa2 (S26A) were pcADV-EF1-mNeonGreen-CMV-Anxa2(S26D)-3xFLAG and pcADV-EF1-mNeonGreen-CMV-Anxa2(S26A)-3xFLAG.
Echocardiography
Mice were anesthetized with a combination of 1.5 % isoflurane and 0.5 L/min of 100 % O
2
, followed by depilation to prepare the skin. The limbs and heart were coated with coupling agent, and the heart structure and function of the mice from each group were detected with an ultra-high resolution small animal ultrasound (Vevo 2100, VisualSonics, Canada). The parasternal left ventricular long axis section was used; the ultrasonic probe was placed at the left ventricular papillary muscle position, and the probe position was moved to obtain a clearer image. M−mode ultrasonic images were collected. Ultrasonic analysis software was used to measure and calculate the cardiac function indexes of mice from each group, including heart rate (HR), fractional shortening (FS), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular end diastolic volume (LVEDV), and left ventricular end systolic volume (LVESV).
RNA extraction, library construction, and sequencing
Total RNA was extracted using a TTRIZOL reagent kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA quality was assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA) and RNase free agarose gel electrophoresis. After total RNA was extracted, mRNA was enriched with Oligo(dT) beads. Then, the enriched mRNA was fragmented into short fragments using fragmentation buffer and reverse transcribed into cDNA using NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB #7530, New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA). The purified double-stranded cDNA fragments were end repaired, and A base was added and ligated to Illumina sequencing adapters. The ligation reaction was purified with AMPure XP Beads (1.0X). Ligated fragments were subjected to size selection by agarose gel electrophoresis and PCR amplified. The resulting cDNA library was sequenced using Illumina Novaseq6000 by Gene Denovo Biotechnology Co. (Guangzhou, China).
Proteomics
Proteins were extracted from the samples and digested enzymatically. Quality control was performed on the samples before mass spectrometry detection. The data obtained from the DDA acquisition mode were used to build a database using Pulsar software. The DIA data results were analyzed using the DDA reference database to identify the proteins. If at least one sample had a detected protein, the qualitative result of the protein and its quantitative results for all samples were output. The qualitative protein analysis required that the identification standards of Precursor Threshold 1.0 % FDR and Protein Threshold 1.0 % FDR at the peptide and protein levels, respectively, were met. Regarding protein quantification, normalization was performed first, and the average peak area of the top 3 MS1 peptides with an FDR less than 1.0 % was selected for protein quantification (GENE DENOVO, Guangzhou, China).

(COIP/MS)
Immunoprecipitation was performed using an anti-ADAM8 antibody (IP: ADAM8) or IgG (IP: IgG) and H293T cells, and the protein lysates were used for Shotgun LC-MS/MS (Genechem Co., Ltd, Shanghai). Ltd, Shanghai). Peptides ionized in a mass spectrometer carry a certain amount of charge, allowing for the determination of their mass-to-charge ratio (
m
/
z
) through the detector. Additionally, peptides were subjected to further ionization and fragmentation in a mass spectrometer, resulting in second-order mass spectrometry signals. By using retrieval software and relevant protein databases, the mass spectrometry data obtained could be analyzed to reconstruct the protein composition of the sample. COIP validation of binding between ADAM8 and ANXA2 was also performed using anti-ADAM8 antibody (IP: ADAM8), ANXA2 antibody (IP: ANXA2), or IgG (IP: IgG) and RAW 264.7 cells. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
(ELISA)
Cell culture supernatants and human plasma samples were centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 20 min at 2–8 ℃ to remove impurities and cell debris. An ELISA was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Wuhan, China), and the optical density (OD) value was measured at a wavelength of 450 nm.
siRNA transfection
siRNA transfection was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (GenePharma, Shanghai, China). The siRNA-Mate transfection reagent was placed at room temperature and gently mixed before use. Next, 100 μL of DMEM (serum-free and antibiotic-free medium) was added to sterile Eppendorf tubes. The appropriate siRNA was added to the Eppendorf tube and mixed thoroughly. Then, the appropriate siRNA-Mate transfection reagent was added and rapidly swirled for 10 s to completely mix. After incubation at room temperature for 10 min, a transfection complex of siRNA and the transfection reagent formed. The cell culture plate was loaded with 0.5 mL of preheated fresh culture medium in each well, and the transfection mixture was added. Then, cells were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h and ANXA2 was knocked down in BMDMs by means of siRNA transfection.
Statistics
The sample size of patients in the clinical cohort and that of mice used in the study was determined based on similar published articles. Strict exclusion criteria were implemented to control confounding factors in the clinical cohort, thereby enhancing the credibility of the study results. Mouse littermates were randomly allocated to different groups, and investigators were blinded to group allocation. SPSS 26.0, GraphPad Prism 9.5.0, and MedCalc 15.0 software were used for data analysis. For continuous data, the data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation. If the data satisfy both normal distribution and homogeneity of variance, the unpaired
t
-test is used for comparisons between two groups, and One-way ANOVA along with Tukey's multiple comparisons test or Student-Newman-Keuls test are employed for comparing more than two groups. If the data satisfy normal distribution but not homogeneity of variance, the unpaired
t
-test with Welch's correction is used for comparisons between two groups, and Welch's ANOVA test is applied for comparisons among multiple groups. If the data do not satisfy normal distribution, the Mann Whitney test is used for comparisons between two groups, and the Kruskal-Wallis test is employed for comparisons among multiple groups. For categorical variables, the chi-squared test was used for comparison. Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the differences between two survival curves were compared using the log-rank test. Statistical details were listed in the
Supplemental Material 2
. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Discussion
The role of the ADAM family in cardiovascular disease remains unclear. The bioinformatic analysis of gene datasets from patients and mice with AMI revealed that ADAM8, first discovered in macrophages, may be a promising therapeutic candidate for AMI. Here, we demonstrated that macrophage-specific ADAM8 deficiency can improve cardiac function, reduce scar formation, and increase the survival rates of mice after MI. Moreover, it was identified that ANXA2 as a binding molecule of ADAM8 that regulates the downstream autophagy pathway, and further affects inflammation and angiogenesis. These findings not only reveal the role of ADAM8 in MI but also shed new light on the mechanistic ability of macrophages to regulate heart function.
Firstly, through analysis of public dataset sequencing of blood samples from MI patients, it was found that ADAM8 is the most significantly altered molecule among the ADAM family in plasma after MI. The present cohort study showed that ADAM8 expression was significantly increased in patients with AMI when compared with the normal group. Through analysis of single-cell transcriptome sequencing datasets from mice and experimental validation, it was found that ADAM8 expression levels were the highest in cardiac macrophages on day 3 after MI in mice, and the degree of the change was significantly higher compared to that of other ADAM family molecules. Therefore, it is believed that ADAM8 in macrophages may play an important role in the progression of MI.
Typically, after a MI occurs, the infarcted area experiences ischemia and hypoxia, leading to local myocardial cell necrosis, increased inflammation, elevated fibrosis levels, suppressed angiogenesis, and adverse ventricular remodeling
[36]
. The macrophage-specific ADAM8 knockout mice that were constructed exhibited improved cardiac function and increased survival rates, along with reduced fibrosis levels and increased angiogenesis. Conversely, AAV-mediated macrophage-specific overexpression mice showed deteriorated cardiac function and decreased survival rates. Bone marrow transplantation experiments further supported these conclusions. However, in our study, it was found that macrophage ADAM8 knockout did not affect the level of early cardiomyocyte apoptosis after MI. The most significant finding of our study was that angiogenesis in the infarcted area was enhanced by macrophage-specific ADAM8 KO after MI. Angiogenesis refers to the process of forming new blood vessels formation from existing capillaries or post-capillary veins. In ischemic heart disease, angiogenesis is crucial for improving myocardial ischemia and promoting myocardial repair
[37]
. By forming new collateral circulation, angiogenesis provides nutrients and oxygen to the ischemic myocardium, alleviates myocardial ischemia, promotes the survival and repair of myocardial cells, and reduces the degree of myocardial fibrosis. Inspired by several studies in which bevacizumab was used, a monoclonal VEGFA antibody recommended for clinical application in cancer, to intervene in mouse models of liver fibrosis
[38]
or retinopathy
[39]
,
[40]
, which significantly inhibited VEGF/VEGFR signaling; we used bevacizumab to treat ADAM8 KO mice with AMI. Taken together, the results clearly showed that angiogenesis inhibition by bevacizumab can exacerbate changes in heart function and reduce the survival rates of ADAM8 KO mice.
Next, it was examined how ADAM8 regulates macrophage function to exert its effects. ADAM8 KO reduced inflammatory factor levels and increased VEGFA levels. RNA sequencing showed that regardless of whether LPS or IL-4 was used, autophagy was an important overlapping pathway. The autophagy-related proteins LC3II/I were increased, and p62 was decreased after ADAM8 KO. The autophagy inhibitor 3MA was then used in ADAM8 KO BMDMs, and it reversed the inflammation and angiogenesis changes induced by ADAM8 KO. Enhanced autophagy in macrophages is known to precede inflammation factor production
[41]
,
[42]
via regulating the inflammasome pathway by mediating the degradation of inflammatory activators or components
[43]
. CXCR4 deficiency in macrophages can reduce the expression of the negative angiogenesis regulatory molecule, decorin, and promote angiogenesis in the ischemic hindlimb by enhancing autophagy
[44]
. Furthermore, cellular autophagy can promote tumor angiogenesis in glioblastoma
[45]
. Thus, autophagy may be a downstream pathway through which ADAM8 controls inflammation and angiogenesis.
Next, the specific mechanism through which ADAM8 regulates autophagy was investigated. Using COIP/MS experiments, ANXA2 was found to be an important binding protein. ADAM8 KO does not affect the mRNA and protein expression levels of ANXA2, but ANXA2 Ser26 was significantly decreased by ADAM8 KO, and there were no differences in ANXA Tyr24 expression. Some studies have reported its indirect effects on gene expression through interactions with other transcription factors. For example, ANXA2 interacts with the thioredoxin-binding domain of DBT, activating the Hippo signal, which leads to reduced nuclear localization of the Yes1-associated transcriptional regulator (YAP) and transcriptional repression of adipogenic genes
[46]
. In this study, since there was no difference in the mRNA level of ANXA2, we did not prioritize the role of ANXA2 in regulating other transcription factors. Our experiments have confirmed that ADAM8 can bind to ANXA2, affecting its phosphorylation level and thereby influencing downstream signaling pathways. Further knockdown of ANXA2 using siRNA can reverse the phenotype of ADAM8 KO. It was found that this may also be due to the reduction of ANXA2 Ser26 phosphorylation after ANXA2 knockdown. Ser26 phosphorylation could induce a conformational switch leading to the dissociation of C-NTD from the CTD, causing a cascade of structural changes and leading to a fully “autoinhibited open state” for the hyper-phosphorylated ANXA2
[47]
. The phosphorylation state of Ser26 plays an important role in the modulation of ANXA2 structure. Tyr24 phosphorylation can anchor the NTD to the core to inhibit membrane aggregation
[47]
. In general, the Ser26 phosphorylation of ANXA2 is crucial for ADAM8.
It is well known that ADAM8, as a metalloprotease, possesses proteolytic functions similar to other family molecules such as ADAM17, but this does not explain its role in binding and phosphorylating ANXA2
[48]
,
[49]
. Previous studies have shown that in microglia, ADAM8 can directly interact with Fra-1 (encoded by the Fosl-1 gene) through its cytoplasmic tail region, therby promoting the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of Fra-1, and upregulating the expression of Map3k4, resulting in exacerbating neuroinflammatory responses
[29]
. ADAM8 can also interact with molecules such as β1 integrin through its disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains, promoting trophoblast cell migration and adhesion through a mechanism independent of proteolytic activity
[50]
. Therefore, in this study, we hypothesize that ADAM8 also binds to ANXA2 and promotes ANXA2 phosphorylation through a mechanism independent of proteolytic activity. Furthermore, using molecular docking platforms, a molecular basis for direct binding between ADAM8 and ANXA2 was discovered, and both the disintegrin and cytoplasmic tail domains of ADAM8 have the potential to simultaneously bind to ANXA2 and protein kinases or phosphatases.
We further constructed adenovirus vectors for Anxa2 Ser26 with sustained phosphorylation inactivation and activation for BMDM transfer experiments, and the role of the Ser26 site in ANXA2 was further validated. Activation of the ANXA2 Ser26 site promoted IL-1β/IL-18/TNF-α shedding and decreased VEGFA secretion, and this trend was reversed by ANXA2 Ser26 site inactivation. mTOR and AMPK can negatively and positively regulate autophagy, respectively. Activated AMPK can inhibit the activity of mTOR, thus promoting the formation of autophagosomes
[51]
. mTORC1 phosphorylates and inactivates the autophagy regulatory complex, thereby affecting the biogenesis of autophagosomes
[52]
. Surprisingly, the phosphorylation of the mTOR Ser2448 site was significantly decreased in KO BMDMs, which was reversed by activation of ANXA2 Ser26 site phosphorylation. Together, these results showed ANXA2 Ser26 site phosphorylation promotes the phosphorylation of mTOR in ADAM8 KO BMDMs. In fact, ANXA2 may promote mTOR phosphorylation in bovine mammary epithelial cells
[53]
. ANXA2 can regulate autophagy via the Akt1-mTOR-ULK1/2 pathway
[54]
. Mukhopadhyay, et al. also showed that ANXA2 can regulate mTOR-dependent autophagy fluctuations
[55]
. Although ANXA2 can also participate in the regulation of β-catenin/TFEB or Hippo pathway
[46]
,
[56]
. In our study, it is highlighted that ADAM8 can regulate mTOR-dependent autophagy via binding to ANXA2; ADAM8 knockout in macrophages can impede ANXA2 Ser26 site phosphorylation, inhibit mTOR Ser2448 site phosphorylation, and activate the autophagy pathway. Subsequently, the secretion of proangiogenic factors is induced, and inflammatory cytokines are inhibited.
In summary, our data indicates that the ADAM8-ANXA2-mTOR-autophagy axis is a key mechanism that regulates angiogenesis and inflammation post-MI, and ADAM8 may be a potential important therapeutic target in MI.
